title: Negotiating and solving problems
cando: negotiate, set conditions and reach an agreement both sides accept

about.text: In this lesson you negotiate a delivery with a supplier, set conditions and look for a compromise that both sides can accept. You also read a set of terms and conditions, write an email proposing a fair solution, and then negotiate a real deal: a price, a date and a condition.
goals: Put forward ideas and ask for more: What if we…? Would you consider…?
Set conditions with provided that, as long as, unless and supposing.
Link two changes in one sentence: The more you order, the lower the price.
Read terms and conditions, and write an email proposing a compromise.
Negotiate a price, a date and a condition that works for both sides.

chapters.title: Meeting halfway
chapters.text:
In this lesson, you negotiate. You set conditions, and you reach an agreement that both sides can accept.
First, you listen to Priya. She buys supplies for a small chain of cafés, and they're opening a new branch. She's on a call with Tomasz, from their coffee supplier.
Priya wants a lower price. Tomasz wants a bigger order. Neither of them gets everything, and that's the point. A good negotiation ends in a compromise.
Listen for the phrases that move things forward. What if we ordered two hundred kilos? Would you consider twelve pounds a kilo? In return, we could sign for six months.
Notice that nobody simply says no. They say: yes, provided that…

chapters.title: Conditions, and two things that change together
chapters.text:
Now the grammar. There are two points.
First, the words that set a condition. Provided that, and as long as, mean only if. We'll deliver on the twenty-eighth, provided that you confirm by Friday.
Unless means if not. Unless you confirm by Friday, I can't promise the date. Don't add another not. Unless already has one inside it.
Supposing, and what if, put an idea on the table. Supposing we split the difference?
Here's the trap. After provided, as long as and unless, use the present, even when you mean the future. As long as you confirm. Not: as long as you will confirm.
Second: the more, the better. The more you order, the lower the price. Both halves start with the, and then a comparative.

chapters.title: Reading the small print
chapters.text:
Next, you read a supplier's terms and conditions.
Terms are written in numbered clauses. Don't read them like a story. Use them like a map, and find the clause you need.
Ask three questions. What must I do? What am I entitled to? And what happens if something goes wrong: a penalty, a discount, or a replacement at no extra cost?
Look out for provided, unless and as long as. That's usually where the real condition is.
Then you write an email that proposes a compromise. Say what happened, name the clause, suggest a solution, and offer something in return.

chapters.title: Your negotiation
chapters.text:
Then it's your turn to negotiate, in the live class or with Wehel.
Your company needs three hundred T-shirts for a charity race. The price is too high, and the delivery date is too late. You must agree a price, a date and one condition.
Prepare before you start. Know your ideal price, and your limit. Decide what you can offer in return: a deposit, or collecting the shirts yourself.
Stay polite, and stay firm. If they won't budge on the price, change the question. Talk about the date, or the payment, instead.
And at the end, sum up the deal. So, just to check…

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article about a negotiation.
Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice what each side wanted, and what each side gave up.
Ask yourself: was the final deal fair? Would you have done anything differently?

warmup.prompt: You want a better price from a supplier. What do you do first?
choices: ask for a discount straight away
say you'll go to another supplier
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many good negotiators start by finding out what the other side needs, because that tells them what they can offer in return.

conversation.title: Negotiating a delivery
conversation.setting: Priya Nair buys supplies for Greenleaf Cafés, a small chain that is about to open a new branch. She's on a video call with Tomasz, a sales manager at their coffee supplier, Harbour Roasters.
lines: Tomasz
Thanks for making time, Priya. So, you're looking at a bigger order for the new branch?
Priya
That's right. But at fourteen pounds a kilo, the numbers don't work for us. We need to get the price down.
Tomasz
Well, the more you order, the lower the price. The bulk price is thirteen pounds a kilo, with a minimum of 200 kilos.
Priya
What if we ordered 200 kilos, but took it in two deliveries? We don't have much storage space.
Tomasz
That's fine, provided that each delivery is at least 100 kilos. But you'd pay shipping on both, because they're smaller deliveries.
Priya
Would you consider twelve pounds a kilo? In return, we could sign up for six months instead of three.
Tomasz
Twelve is below our costs, so I can't budge that far. Supposing we split the difference: twelve fifty, for a six-month deal?
Priya
I can go along with that, as long as shipping is included on at least one delivery.
Tomasz
All right, I'll include it on the first. And the date?
Priya
We open on the first of October, so the first delivery must arrive by the twenty-eighth.
Tomasz
Unless the order's confirmed by Friday, I can't promise the twenty-eighth.
Priya
You'll have it by Thursday. So, just to check: twelve fifty a kilo, two deliveries of 100 kilos, free shipping on the first, and a six-month agreement.
Tomasz
That's it. I think that's a win-win deal.
Priya
So do I. Thanks for meeting us halfway, Tomasz. I'll put it all in an email today.

questions.a: The order must be confirmed by Friday.

Priya must order more than 200 kilos.

items.meaning: To discuss something with somebody until you both agree, for example on a price, a salary or a date.
items.example: We negotiated a lower rent for the second year.

items.meaning: An agreement in which each side accepts a little less than it wanted.
items.example: Neither of us got everything, but it was a fair compromise.

items.meaning: An agreement, especially in business, in which both sides get something.
items.example: We've signed a two-year deal with a new cleaning company.

items.meaning: A company that sells goods, such as food, parts or paper, to another business.
items.example: Our supplier has put its prices up again.

items.meaning: A large quantity. If you buy in bulk, you buy a lot at once, usually at a lower price.
items.example: We buy printer paper in bulk because it's much cheaper.

items.meaning: The smallest amount that is allowed or needed.
items.example: There's a minimum of fifty units per order.

items.meaning: Sending goods to a customer, and the cost of sending them.
items.example: Shipping is free on orders over £100.

items.meaning: Good for both sides, so that nobody loses.
items.example: It's a win-win situation: they get steady work, and we get a better price.

items.meaning: To reach a compromise, where each side gives up part of what it wanted.
items.example: If you can deliver a week earlier, we'll meet you halfway on the price.

items.meaning: To agree on an amount exactly between two offers.
items.example: You say £60 and I say £40, so let's split the difference and call it £50.

items.meaning: As an exchange for something that somebody gives you or does for you.
items.example: We'll pay in advance, and in return we'd like a five per cent discount.

items.meaning: To suggest an idea or a plan so that other people can consider it.
items.example: She put forward a plan to share the delivery costs.

items.meaning: To accept an idea or a decision, often after some doubt.
items.example: I wasn't sure about the new schedule at first, but I'll go along with it.

items.meaning: To stop demanding something, or to accept that you cannot win an argument.
items.example: The landlord backed down and agreed to fix the heating.

items.meaning: To change your position or opinion, even a little. It is usually used with not.
items.example: We asked for a discount, but they wouldn't budge.

sound.title: Up at the comma, down at the end
sound.explain: A condition sentence has two halves. When the condition comes first, your voice rises a little at the comma: it tells the listener that you haven't finished. It falls at the end. When the condition comes second, there's no rise in the middle. The dot shows where your voice rises. Listen, then say each line.
groups: Provided that you confirm by Friday · we can deliver on the 28th
As long as shipping is included · I can go along with that
Unless the order's confirmed by Friday · I can't promise the date
lines: We can deliver on the 28th provided that you confirm by Friday.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Four of them set a condition or suggest an idea. The first one links two changes.
examples: The more you order, the lower the price.
That's fine, provided that each delivery is at least 100 kilos.
I can go along with that, as long as shipping is included.
Unless the order's confirmed by Friday, I can't promise the twenty-eighth.
Supposing we split the difference: twelve fifty, for a six-month deal?
spot.question: Which word means 'if not'? Which two mean 'only if'? Which one puts an idea on the table? And is the verb after them present or future?
spot.answer: Unless means 'if not': if the order isn't confirmed, there's no promise. Provided that and as long as mean 'only if'. Supposing puts forward an idea. The verb after them is present (is, is included, 's confirmed), although every sentence is about the future. The first sentence links two changes with the more…, the lower…

rules.title: Setting conditions: provided that, as long as, unless, supposing
rule: Provided (that) and as long as mean 'only if': We'll deliver on the 28th, provided that you confirm by Friday.
Unless means 'if not': Unless you confirm by Friday, we can't promise the 28th.
Supposing or What if + past puts forward an idea: Supposing we ordered more, would the price come down?
After provided, as long as and unless, use the present for the future: as long as you pay, not as long as you will pay.
Provided that is firmer and more formal. As long as is everyday English.
rules.mistake: Not: Unless you won't confirm by Friday… Say: Unless you confirm by Friday… (unless already means 'if not').

rules.title: The more…, the lower…
rule: The + comparative, the + comparative: two things change together.
The more you order, the lower the price.
The sooner you confirm, the sooner we can deliver.
The longer we wait, the more it will cost.
A short form for replies: The sooner, the better.
rules.mistake: Not: More you order, lower the price. Say: The more you order, the lower the price.

practice.q: You'll get the bulk price ___ you order at least 200 kilos.
practice.why: Provided that means 'only if': the price depends on the size of the order.

practice.q: ___ you confirm by Friday, we can't promise the 28th.
practice.why: Unless means 'if not': no confirmation, no promise.

practice.q: As long as the goods ___ on time, we'll sign the contract.
practice.why: After as long as, use the present, even about the future.

practice.q: ___ we split the difference? Would that work for you?
practice.why: Supposing puts forward an idea for the other side to consider.

practice.q: We can't lower the price unless you ___ a longer contract.
practice.why: Unless already means 'if not', so there is no don't, and no will.

practice.q: What if we ___ 300 kilos instead of 200?
practice.why: What if + past makes a polite, tentative suggestion.

practice.q: You can borrow the display stand ___ you bring it back by Monday.
practice.why: As long as means 'only if': bringing it back is the condition.

practice.q: The more you order, ___ the price.
practice.why: Both halves need the + a comparative.

practice.q: The ___ you pay, the bigger the discount.
The longer we wait, ___ it will cost.
practice.why: The + comparative in both halves: the longer…, the more…

yourTurn.prompt: A client asks your team to finish a project a week early. Agree, but set three conditions. Finish with one sentence that uses the sooner…, the… or the more…, the…
starters: We can do it, provided that …
yourTurn.model: We can finish a week early, provided that you send us the final designs by Monday. As long as nothing else changes, the extra hours won't cost you more. Unless we hear from you by Wednesday, we'll keep the original date. The sooner you confirm, the easier it is for us to plan.

text.title: Harbour Roasters: terms of supply
text.body:
PRACTICE DOCUMENT: this company does not exist

HARBOUR ROASTERS LTD
Terms of supply for business customers (extract)

1. Orders
1.1 The minimum order is 50 kg. Orders of 200 kg or more are charged at the bulk price and may be delivered in two parts.
1.2 Each order must specify the quantity, the blend and the delivery address. We cannot accept orders by phone alone.

2. Delivery and shipping
2.1 We aim to deliver within five working days of confirming your order.
2.2 If a delivery is more than three working days late, you are entitled to a 10% discount on that delivery.
2.3 Shipping is included at no extra cost on deliveries of 150 kg or more. Smaller deliveries are charged £18 each.

3. Payment
3.1 Payment is due within 30 days of the invoice date.
3.2 Orders over £2,000 may be paid in instalments, provided that the first instalment is paid on delivery.
3.3 A penalty of 2% a month is added to any amount still outstanding after 30 days.
3.4 Unless all outstanding invoices are paid, we may hold back new deliveries.

4. Equipment and faults
4.1 Every coffee machine we supply comes with a 12-month warranty covering parts and labour.
4.2 The warranty does not cover damage caused by misuse, or by repairs carried out by anyone other than our own engineers.
4.3 Damaged goods must be reported within seven days of delivery. As long as you report them in time, we will replace them at no extra cost.

5. Obligations
5.1 Your obligations: to check each delivery when it arrives, and to store coffee in a cool, dry place.
5.2 Our obligations: to deliver the goods you ordered, on time and in good condition.

6. Changes to these terms
Either side may ask to change these terms. Any change must be agreed in writing, and we will draw up a new agreement for both sides to sign.

an advert for a new coffee machine

items.meaning: One numbered part of a contract or a set of terms.
items.example: Clause 3 explains how and when you have to pay.

items.meaning: Something you must do because a law, a contract or a promise says so.
items.example: Checking each delivery is one of the customer's obligations.

items.meaning: Having the right to have or to do something.
items.example: If the train is more than an hour late, you're entitled to a refund.

items.meaning: A written promise to repair or replace a product if it goes wrong within a set time.
items.example: The printer comes with a two-year warranty.

items.meaning: One of several payments you make over time, until the full amount is paid.
items.example: We're paying for the new van in twelve monthly instalments.

items.meaning: An amount you must pay, or a punishment, for breaking a rule or an agreement.
items.example: There's a penalty if you pay the invoice late.

items.meaning: Not paid or not done yet.
items.example: We still have two invoices outstanding from March.

items.meaning: Included in the price, so you don't pay any more for it.
items.example: They replaced the broken part at no extra cost.

items.meaning: To say or write exactly what you want or need.
items.example: Please specify the size and the colour when you order.

items.meaning: To write a contract, a plan or a list carefully, in the correct form.
items.example: Our lawyer will draw up the new agreement next week.

model.title: An email proposing a compromise
model.body:
Subject: Our second delivery: a proposal

Dear Tomasz,

Thank you for your email about our second delivery. I understand that your driver took it to our head office instead of the new branch, and that this is why it arrived four working days late.

We did give the branch address on our order, as clause 1.2 requires, so we believe we are entitled to the 10% discount in clause 2.2. However, I can see that our account still showed head office as the delivery address, and keeping the account up to date was partly our obligation.

Rather than argue about it, I would like to put forward a compromise. Could we split the difference and agree a 5% discount on that delivery? In return, we are happy to pay the invoice this week, instead of at the end of the month.

If you can go along with this, please could you send a corrected invoice that specifies the discount? The sooner this is settled, the sooner we can both move on to the next order.

Kind regards,
Priya Nair
Purchasing Manager, Greenleaf Cafés

write.task: Write an email of 150 to 200 words that proposes a compromise. Use a real problem with a supplier, a landlord, a client or your employer, or invent one. Say what happened and what the terms say. Then put forward a compromise, and offer something in return.
checklist: I said what happened, and which clause or rule applies.
I put forward a compromise and offered something in return.
I used at least two of: provided that, as long as, unless, the sooner…, the…
I asked for a clear next step and closed the email politely.

card.title: Agree the deal
card.situation: Your company is running a charity race and needs 300 printed T-shirts. The printer quotes £9 a shirt and five weeks for delivery. You'd like to pay £8 a shirt, and your limit is £8.50. The race is on 15 June, and you need the shirts by 10 June, which is four weeks from today.
card.goal: Agree a price, a delivery date and one condition that works for both sides. Offer something in return for what you ask for.

phrases: We'd like to go ahead, but we're over budget.
What if we paid half now, as a deposit?
Would you consider eight pounds a shirt?
I can go along with that, as long as …
prepare.notes: Before you start, write down three things: your ideal price, your limit and your latest possible date. Then list what you can offer in return: a deposit, collecting the shirts yourself, a quick decision or another order next year.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is the printer. Negotiate the order and agree a price, a date and one condition. Then change roles, or negotiate with another learner and compare your deals.
doIt.wehel: You are Lena, a sales manager at a company that prints T-shirts. I want 300 T-shirts for a charity race. Your price is £9 a shirt, and delivery takes five weeks. Do not agree at once. Ask me for something in return, like a deposit or more time. At the end, we must agree a price, a date and one condition. Then tell me one thing I did well and one thing to improve.

model.title: The deal
lines: Lena
Thanks for getting back to me. So, 300 shirts for the charity race?
You
That's right. We'd like to go ahead, but at nine pounds a shirt we're over budget. Is there any room on the price?
Lena
Not a lot, I'm afraid. The price includes printing on both sides.
You
What if we paid half now, as a deposit? Would you consider eight pounds a shirt?
Lena
Eight is too low for me. Supposing we split the difference: eight fifty?
You
I can go along with eight fifty, as long as the date works. We need the shirts by the tenth.
Lena
The tenth is only four weeks away, and we normally need five.
You
We could collect the shirts ourselves. Would that save you some time?
Lena
It saves two days. All right: the tenth, provided that we have your final design by Monday.
You
Monday is fine. One more thing: we'd like to see a sample shirt before you print all 300.
Lena
Of course. I'll send one by Wednesday, as long as the design arrives on Monday.
You
Great. So, just to check: 300 shirts at eight fifty, half paid now, the design by Monday, a sample by Wednesday, and we collect on the tenth.
Lena
That's the deal. I'll draw up the order and send it this afternoon.
compare: Did you offer something in return for what you asked for?
Did you set or accept a condition with provided that, as long as or unless?
Did you agree a price, a date and a condition?
Did you sum up the deal at the end: So, just to check…?

canDo: I can put forward ideas and offer something in return.
I can set conditions with provided that, as long as, unless and supposing.
I can read terms and conditions and find what I'm entitled to.
I can write an email proposing a compromise.
I can negotiate a price, a date and a condition that both sides accept.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is negotiating, and what do you think each side wants?
reading.talk: Did both sides get a fair deal in the end? Think of a time you negotiated something: a price, a rent, a salary or a deadline. What did you give, and what did you get? Write a short paragraph, or talk about it with Wehel.

quiz.q: We'll deliver on the 28th ___ you confirm the order by Friday.
quiz.why: Provided that means 'only if': the date depends on the confirmation.

quiz.q: ___ you pay within 30 days, a penalty is added to the invoice.
quiz.why: Unless means 'if not': if you don't pay in time, you pay a penalty.

quiz.q: The sooner you order, ___ we can deliver.
quiz.why: Both halves need the + a comparative.

quiz.q: We asked for a discount, but they wouldn't ___ on the price.
quiz.why: Won't budge means won't change their position at all.

quiz.q: You say £60 and I say £40. Let's ___ the difference: £50.
quiz.why: Split the difference means agree on the amount halfway between two offers.

quiz.q: The machine broke after six months, so the ___ covered the repair.
quiz.why: A warranty is a promise to repair or replace a product for a set time.

quiz.q: Two invoices from March are still ___ . We haven't paid them yet.
quiz.why: Outstanding means not paid or not done yet.

quiz.q: ___, the trial was short. Even so, the results were clear.
quiz.why: Admittedly accepts a weak point before you answer it with even so.

quiz.q: Sales rose in the north, ___ they fell in the south.
quiz.why: Whereas contrasts two facts in one sentence.

quiz.q: Cheaper bus fares are likely to ___ fewer cars in the town centre.
quiz.why: Lead to means cause: the cheaper fares come first, then fewer cars.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the delivery negotiation in pairs, then change the product, the numbers and the date. Every pair must use provided that, unless and the more…, the…
Day 2: the negotiation role-play. You are the printer, and each learner agrees a price, a date and a condition with you. Then pairs negotiate with each other, and the class compares the deals.
Day 3: talk about the book. Then two learners read their compromise emails aloud, and the group decides whether each proposal is fair to both sides.
